power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .112", "p = .112"), Sentence = c("In the CFA, the one-factor model was rejected (CFI = .894, RMSEA = .079), whereas the three-factor model fitted well, χ²ss(186) = 209.7, p = .112, CFI = .996, TLI = .995, RMSEA = .016, 90% CI [.000, .026], SRMR = .037.", "Reliability α = .91, 95% CI [.90, .92]; ordinal ω total = .95; ωh = .79; ECV = .66 -Number of factors Parallel analysis: 3; MAP test: 3 3 One-factor CFA χ²ss(189) = 769.8, CFI = .894, RMSEA = .079 Misspecified Property Result from PsyScale Studio Generating model Three-factor CFA χ²ss(186) = 209.7, p = .112, CFI = .996, TLI = .995, RMSEA = .016 [.000, .026], SRMR = .037" )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: The analysis code, example data and verification scripts are provided as supplementary material.
The authors wrote a handbook on scale development published by UMS Press, which the application follows.
PsyScale Studio was developed by the authors and is free of charge; the authors receive no income from it.
See the Declarations for details.
This work received no specific funding.
Questionnaires and tests are the main instruments of health, social and behavioral research, and their scores are only as useful as the evidence that they measure what they claim to measure.

Current standards describe validation as the accumulation of evidence from several sources: test content, response processes, internal structure, relations to other variables and the consequences of testing (American Educational Research Association et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Current standards describe validation as the accumulation of evidence from several sources: test content, response processes, internal structure, relations to other variables and the consequences of testing <ref type="bibr">(American Educational Research Association et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In practice, a validation study for a new or adapted scale requires a long sequence of analyses: content validity indices, data screening, classical item analysis, reliability, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, Rasch or item response theory (IRT) models, differential item functioning (DIF), measurement invariance, test-retest reliability and correlations with external criteria (Boateng et al., 2018; Prinsen et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In practice, a validation study for a new or adapted scale requires a long sequence of analyses: content validity indices, data screening, classical item analysis, reliability, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, Rasch or item response theory (IRT) models, differential item functioning (DIF), measurement invariance, test-retest reliability and correlations with external criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Boateng et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Prinsen et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these analyses is well supported by statistical software.

R packages such as psych (Revelle, 2024), lavaan (Rosseel, 2012), semTools (Jorgensen et al., 2022), mirt (Chalmers, 2012), eRm (Mair & Hatzinger, 2007) and CDM (George et al., 2016) implement current methods, and menu-driven programs such as JASP (Love et al., 2019) make several of them accessible without code.
text.formatted: R packages such as psych <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Revelle, 2024)</ref>, lavaan <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Rosseel, 2012)</ref>, semTools <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Jorgensen et al., 2022)</ref>, mirt <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chalmers, 2012)</ref>, eRm <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Mair & Hatzinger, 2007)</ref> and CDM <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(George et al., 2016)</ref> implement current methods, and menu-driven programs such as JASP <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Love et al., 2019</ref>) make several of them accessible without code.

text.text: The difficulty for many applied researchers, and especially for graduate students, lies elsewhere: deciding which analyses a particular study needs and in what order, choosing estimators suited to ordinal items, reading the output against defensible criteria, and reporting the results correctly.

Errors at these points are common, for example treating Likert items as continuous in confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), reporting coefficient alpha for multidimensional scales, or comparing group means without testing measurement invariance (Rhemtulla et al., 2012; Rodriguez et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Errors at these points are common, for example treating Likert items as continuous in confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), reporting coefficient alpha for multidimensional scales, or comparing group means without testing measurement invariance <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Rhemtulla et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Rodriguez et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: PsyScale Studio was developed to close this gap.

It is a web application that (a) builds an analysis roadmap from the purpose of the study and the response format of the scale, (b) runs each analysis with established methods, using R itself for the model-based analyses, (c) explains every result in plain language with criteria and references, and (d) assembles an APAstyle report together with the exact R code needed to reproduce it.
All computation happens inside the user's web browser, so research data are never uploaded.

This article describes the design and implementation of the application, evaluates the accuracy of its statistical engines against R, and illustrates the workflow with a simulated scale whose true properties are known and with a public dataset for cognitive diagnosis.
Four principles guided the design.

First, the workflow follows the sources of validity evidence in the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (American Educational Research Association et al., 2014) and the measurement properties of the COSMIN taxonomy (Prinsen et al., 2018), and the order of steps follows a practical handbook on scale development (Assis et al., 2026a).
text.formatted: First, the workflow follows the sources of validity evidence in the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing <ref type="bibr">(American Educational Research Association et al., 2014)</ref> and the measurement properties of the COSMIN taxonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Prinsen et al., 2018)</ref>, and the order of steps follows a practical handbook on scale development <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Assis et al., 2026a)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the analyses depend on the study.

Users state whether they are developing a new scale, translating or adapting a scale, or using an existing scale in a new population, and choose one of ten response formats: dichotomous, partial credit, mixed, Likert or rating, semantic differential, unscored multiple choice, continuous (e.g., visual analogue scales), rater-scored, forced choice and formative indices.
These choices determine which steps appear, their order and the estimators used.
Third, every result is explained.
Each statistic is accompanied by a note describing what it is, when to use it, how to read it, what to do if it is poor, an example sentence for a report and references.
Fourth, data privacy is protected by design: datasets are processed in the browser and are never sent to a server.
PsyScale Studio is a single-page web application written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Figure 1).
text.formatted: PsyScale Studio is a single-page web application written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Two statistical engines run inside the browser.

A JavaScript engine computes classical item statistics, reliability coefficients, polychoric and tetrachoric correlations, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), Rasch models estimated by conditional maximum likelihood, dichotomous IRT models and CFA for dichotomous items.
A second engine runs R itself through webR, a version of R compiled to WebAssembly (Stagg & Posit Software, 2026).
text.formatted: A second engine runs R itself through webR, a version of R compiled to WebAssembly <ref type="bibr">(Stagg & Posit Software, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: When an analysis needs R, the browser downloads the webR runtime and the required packages from a public repository; only software is downloaded.
The model-based analyses then run with lavaan, semTools, mirt, CDM and base R. At the time of writing, the browser engine used webR 0.6.0 (R 4.6.0).
The versions of R and of every package used are printed with each result and stored in the reproducibility package.
Note.
All analyses run in the user's web browser.
The account service stores account details only, and the package repository supplies software only; research data are not transmitted.
Access is managed with Google Firebase.

Users register with an email address or a Google account and are approved by an administrator; the account service stores only account details (name, institution, country, position and intended use) and never research data.
A firstvisit tour and an illustrated user guide introduce the interface.
The workflow begins with a Setup step in which users choose the study purpose and response format and load their data from a CSV or Excel file or by pasting from a spreadsheet (Figure 2).
text.formatted: The workflow begins with a Setup step in which users choose the study purpose and response format and load their data from a CSV or Excel file or by pasting from a spreadsheet (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Users then assign column roles (respondent identifier, group variables, item columns and external criteria) and may define subscales.
The application displays a roadmap of steps in the order suited to the stated purpose.
For a new scale, content validity and EFA precede CFA; for an existing scale in a new population, CFA precedes EFA and invariance testing is emphasized.
Steps that do not apply to the chosen format are marked as not applicable rather than hidden, so users can see why an analysis is not offered.
Note.
Users choose the study purpose and the response format and then load their data; the roadmap on the left lists the steps in the order suited to the stated purpose.

Each step page follows the same layout: the reason for the step, what it requires, settings, a Run button, results tables with color-coded criteria, and a box headed "What it means" that interprets the results in APA style (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Each step page follows the same layout: the reason for the step, what it requires, settings, a Run button, results tables with color-coded criteria, and a box headed "What it means" that interprets the results in APA style (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Items can be excluded or restored from the results pages; each decision is recorded with its reason in an item decision log that is included in the report.
A button on each page opens a one-page summary of the corresponding handbook chapter.
Note.
Top: comparison of competing models estimated with lavaan in webR and the standardized loadings of the selected model.
Bottom: the automatically generated interpretation and suggested next steps.
Data are the simulated mental health dataset.
Table 1 lists the analyses by step and the engine that runs them.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> lists the analyses by step and the engine that runs them.

text.text: For ordinal items, CFA uses robust weighted least squares (WLSMV) on polychoric correlations and reports scaled fit statistics; continuous items use robust maximum likelihood (MLR).
The application fits competing models (one factor, correlated factors, second-order and bifactor), flags inadmissible solutions, and reports composite reliability and average variance extracted.

Measurement invariance follows the identification sequence for ordered categorical data proposed by Wu and Estabrook (2016) (configural, thresholds, metric, scalar) and judges each step by the scaled chi-square difference test and the change criteria of Chen (2007) and Cheung and Rensvold (2002).
text.formatted: Measurement invariance follows the identification sequence for ordered categorical data proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Wu and Estabrook (2016)</ref> (configural, thresholds, metric, scalar) and judges each step by the scaled chi-square difference test and the change criteria of <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Chen (2007)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cheung and Rensvold (2002)</ref>.

text.text: Missing data can be handled by listwise deletion or by using all available data (pairwise estimation for WLSMV, full-information maximum likelihood for MLR).
Cognitive diagnostic models compare the DINA, DINO, additive (A-CDM) and generalized DINA models (de la Torre, 2011) using a Q-matrix that users build or paste.

Interpretations are generated from the results with explicit criteria and citations, for example the cutoffs of Hu and Bentler (1999) for CFA, the change criteria for invariance and the criteria of Koo and Li (2016) for intraclass correlations.

text.text: The test data were the complete cases (N = 491) of the simulated mental health dataset described in the next section: 21 items scored 0-3.

The comparisons covered coefficient alpha, corrected item-total correlations, a polychoric correlation, the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) index, EFA loadings, hierarchical and total omega, and the partial credit model for the seven depression items (item locations, conditional log-likelihood, person separation reliability, and infit and outfit mean squares).
Item locations were centered before comparison because eRm and the application anchor the scale differently.
Tolerances were set in advance at a level below the reporting precision of each statistic (Table 2).
text.formatted: Tolerances were set in advance at a level below the reporting precision of each statistic (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The comparison runs inside the application and can be repeated by any user.
For the R-based CFA, the application's R code was run on the same data in R 4.3.3 with lavaan 0.6.17 and compared with a direct lavaan analysis of a three-factor model estimated with WLSMV.
All 12 comparisons of the JavaScript engine were within tolerance (Table 2).
text.formatted: All 12 comparisons of the JavaScript engine were within tolerance (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The largest absolute differences were 1.8 × 10 ¹² for alpha, 8.0 × 10 ⁶ for the EFA loadings and ⁻ ⁻ omega hierarchical, and 2.7 × 10 ⁵ for person separation reliability.
The R-based CFA ⁻ reproduced lavaan to four decimal places for the chi-square statistics, CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR, the standardized loading and its standard error.

The JavaScript CFA, which the application uses only for dichotomous items, reproduced lavaan's standardized loadings within .005 and its SRMR within .001 on the polytomous data, but its scaled chi-square and the indices derived from it differed (e.g., CFI .997 vs. .996); for this reason, CFA for polytomous items is always run in R.

The example uses the dataset built into the application: simulated responses of 600 respondents to 21 items with four response categories (0 = never to3 = almost always), seven items each for depression, anxiety and stress.
Responses were generated from three correlated latent factors (generating correlations .62-.70) with standardized loadings of .62-.80, except item ANX6, which was generated with a loading of .30.
Item STR4 was given DIF by lowering its thresholds by 0.6 for women.
Latent means differed by setting and gender, about 1% of responses were deleted at random, and six respondents gave the same answer to every item.

The dataset also includes a well-being score (generated to correlate about -.75 with the total), a social desirability score (unrelated), a diagnostic status (about 19% cases) and a 14-day retest total for 150 respondents.
Because the data are simulated, no ethics approval was required; the generating script is publicly available (see the Open Practices Statement).

The R-based analyses in this example were run with the application's R code in R 4.3.3 (lavaan 0.6.17, semTools 0.5-6, mirt 1.48) so that the values reported here can be reproduced exactly; in the browser, the same code runs with the package versions available in webR.
The size of the dataset was fixed at 600 respondents (491 complete cases) to resemble a typical validation study, and its adequacy was evaluated a priori with the application's planner.

For the three-factor model (df = 186), N = 491 and α = .05, the power of the RMSEA test of close fit (ε₀ = .05) was .83 against εₐ = .06 and greater than .99 against εₐ = .07 and .08 (MacCallum et al., 1996).
text.formatted: For the three-factor model (df = 186), N = 491 and α = .05, the power of the RMSEA test of close fit (ε₀ = .05) was .83 against εₐ = .06 and greater than .99 against εₐ = .07 and .08 <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(MacCallum et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Power of .80 would have required 454, 158 and 88 respondents for these three alternatives, respectively.

text.text: The data screening step reported 122 missing cells (0.97%) in 109 respondents.

Reliability was high (α = .91, 95% CI [.90, .92]; ordinal ω total = .95), but hierarchical omega (.79) and the explained common variance (.66) were too low to support a unidimensional total score (Rodriguez et al., 2016).

text.text: Parallel analysis and the minimum average partial test both indicated three factors, matching the generating model.

In the CFA, the one-factor model was rejected (CFI = .894, RMSEA = .079), whereas the three-factor model fitted well, χ²ss(186) = 209.7, p = .112, CFI = .996, TLI = .995, RMSEA = .016, 90% CI [.000, .026], SRMR = .037.
The second-order model was statistically equivalent, and the bifactor model fitted only marginally better (CFI = .997).

Item ANX6, generated as the weakest item, had the lowest standardized loading (.45; all other items .62-.81), was the only item outside the Rasch fit range (outfit = 1.51), and was the only item that misfit by the S-X² statistic in the IRT analysis.
The estimated factor correlations (.70-.71) were somewhat higher than the generating values (.62-.70), partly because the group differences in latent means add shared variance.

The R-based analyses were run in R 4.3.3 (lavaan 0.6.17, semTools 0.5-6, mirt 1.48).

Of the 21 items, only STR4 was flagged for gender DIF by both ordinal logistic regression and the standardized mean difference procedure (SMD/SD = -0.34, McFadden ΔR² = .026), which is the item generated with DIF.
The invariance analysis illustrates a known limitation of global criteria.
The changes in CFI and RMSEA from the configural to the scalar model (ΔCFI ≥ -.003, ΔRMSEA ≤ .004) met the usual cutoffs, so the change criteria alone suggested full scalar invariance.
The scaled chi-square difference tests, however, were significant for the metric (Δχ²(18) = 32.1, p = .021) and scalar steps (Δχ²(18) = 34.2, p = .012), consistent with the single item with DIF.
The application reports both kinds of evidence, together with modification indices, so that users can investigate partial invariance.

Relations to other variables matched the generating model: the total score correlated r = -.74, 95% CI [-.77, -.70], with well-being and r = -.05, 95% CI [-.13, .03], with social desirability, and separated diagnostic groups well (Hedges' g = 2.24, 95% CI [2.00, 2.48]; AUC = .924, 95% CI [.899, .949]).
The 14-day test-retest reliability was ICC(2,1) = .95, 95% CI [.93, .96], with a smallest detectable change of 5.75 points.

PsyScale Studio brings the analyses of a scale validation study into a single guided workflow that runs in a web browser.

Its contribution is not new statistical methodology but the integration of established methods into a sequence that follows the purpose of the study, explains each result and produces a report that can be checked and reproduced.

In the illustrative example, the workflow recovered the generating structure, the weak item and the item with DIF, and it reported both global and test-based evidence on invariance rather than a single verdict.
Several limitations should be noted.
First, automated interpretation cannot replace expert judgement.
Criteria such as fit-index cutoffs are conventions, and the application presents them as guides, states where they conflict and encourages users to consult the cited sources.
Second, R analyses need an internet connection the first time, to download the webR runtime and packages, and the first R analysis of a session can take one to three minutes.
Third, computation in the browser is slower than in desktop R, which may limit very large samples or complex models such as multigroup bifactor models.
Fourth, results in the browser depend on the package versions available for webR; the versions are therefore recorded with every result, and small numerical differences between versions are possible.
Fifth, the evaluation reported here concerns numerical accuracy; a formal usability study with students and researchers is planned.
Finally, some analyses are not yet included, among them multilevel factor analysis, longitudinal invariance and responsiveness analyses.
Planned developments include a usability evaluation, further verification datasets, additional languages, and support for responsiveness and multilevel designs.

The application's R-based confirmatory factor analysis (three correlated factors, WLSMV) reproduced lavaan 0.6.17 to four decimal places: χ² = 121.3025, scaled χ² = 209.7199, CFI = 0.9957, TLI = 0.9951, RMSEA = 0.0161, SRMR = 0.0373, standardized loading of DEP1 = 0.7925 (SE = 0.0281).
With Existing SoftwareR packages offer the broadest and most current methods but require programming, and users must decide themselves which analyses to run and how to report them.

Menu-driven programs such as JASP(Love et al., 2019) lower the programming barrier and cover several of the same analyses, but they leave the selection, ordering and interpretation of analyses to the user and do not organize them around the sources of validity evidence.
text.formatted: Menu-driven programs such as JASP<ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Love et al., 2019)</ref> lower the programming barrier and cover several of the same analyses, but they leave the selection, ordering and interpretation of analyses to the user and do not organize them around the sources of validity evidence.

text.text: Specialized commercial programs, for example for structural equation modeling or Rasch analysis, cover one part of the workflow each.

PsyScale Studio differs in three respects: the workflow is organized by study purpose and response format; every result is interpreted with explicit criteria and references; and the model-based analyses run with the same R packages that researchers would use themselves, with the code exported for verification.
Running R in the browser also means that sensitive data, such as clinical questionnaires, never leave the user's computer.
